title: Perceptrons: A First Learning Neuron
subtitle: Understand weights, bias and a decision boundary before a large neural network.
scenario: An automatic recycling sorter learns whether a sensor reading looks like metal or paper.
sections: A neuron computes a weighted sum
A sensor measures brightness and reflectance for a recyclable object.
A perceptron multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias, then applies a simple activation rule.
Multiply each input by its weight

x = [2,1]; w = [1,-1]; bias=-.5
score = sum(a*b for a,b in zip(x,w))+bias
print(score>=0)
A sorter mistakes one sample for metal.
Positive and negative weights pull decisions in different directions; the bias shifts the threshold.
Increasing the brightness weight may move some samples to the 'metal' side.
A perceptron can learn from errors
A labelled training example was misclassified.
A basic perceptron update adjusts weights toward the desired label when a mistake occurs. It is not the same as backpropagation through a multilayer network.
For target 1 and prediction 0, a positive learning rate increases weights along the input vector.

weights = [0.0,0.0]
x=[1,2]; target=1; prediction=0; lr=.1
print([w+lr*(target-prediction)*xi for w,xi in zip(weights,x)])

title: Neural Networks and Training
subtitle: Combine neurons into layers and watch a tiny network improve.
scenario: A handwritten symbol recogniser must distinguish simple patterns that one line cannot separate.
sections: Why a network needs hidden layers
Four 2D points form a checkerboard pattern.
One linear perceptron cannot perfectly represent XOR; combining nonlinear neurons makes richer boundaries possible.
For points (0,0),(1,1) → 0 and (0,1),(1,0) → 1, no single straight line separates the classes.
From input to output: forward pass
Two measurements enter a small neural network.
Each neuron forms a weighted sum plus bias, applies an activation function and sends its result to the next layer.
An input passes through a hidden layer, then an output layer that estimates its class.
Predictions are sometimes wrong during training.
Loss measures mismatch between predictions and known answers. Training updates parameters to reduce the loss across examples.
Squared error for target 1.0 and prediction 0.6 is (1-0.6)^2=0.16.
A model has several layers that contribute to one wrong prediction.
Backpropagation efficiently calculates how changes to each weight affect the loss. Gradient descent then performs a small update.
If increasing a weight increases loss, the update reduces that weight; if it decreases loss, update goes the other way.

title: Revision: Computer Vision and Neural Networks
subtitle: Connect image pixels, learned features and predictions.
scenario: A classroom sketch-recognition demo must be accurate on drawings it has never seen.
sections: A student draws a digit on a small canvas.
Image pixels become input numbers, a preprocessing step rescales them, and a learned classifier predicts a label.
A grayscale 8×8 image contains 64 values; a digit model might use those 64 numbers as features.

image = [[0]*8 for _ in range(8)]
image[3][4]=255
print(image[3][4])
A digit looks different when tilted.
Thresholding filters adjust pixels by a rule; neural networks learn weighted transformations from examples.
Changing brightness can affect a rule-based threshold and the neural model differently.
Identify the source of the difference
A model correctly recognises 18 of 20 held-out digits.
Accuracy = correct / total; a confusion matrix shows which types of mistakes happened. Test data must not be used during training.
18/20=90%, but both mistakes might involve the same digit, so inspect errors by class.

title: Mid-Term Evaluation
subtitle: Demonstrate your understanding through practical tasks and short explanations.
scenario: A small team must assess an ML system before showing it at a school fair.
sections: An evaluator asks whether a solution should use fixed rules, ID3, K-Means or a neural network.
Choose algorithms based on the form of available data and the desired result, not their popularity.
Known class labels → supervised learning; unknown groups → clustering; known sensor rules → conventional programming.
A classifier receives new points and produces labels.
A fair evaluation uses examples that were not included in training and reports results clearly.
If 7 of 10 held-out cases are correct, accuracy is 70%; explain two failures.

predictions=['A','B','A']; actual=['A','A','A']
print(sum(a==b for a,b in zip(predictions,actual)))
The teacher sees a model's answer but does not know how it was produced.
A useful technical explanation names the input, transformation, output and limitation. Diagrams are as valuable as code for this task.
A pixel image becomes a number grid, then hidden neuron activations, then a predicted digit.

title: Generative AI: GPT, Data and Society
subtitle: Tokens, next-word prediction, social-media data, ethics and responsible use.
scenario: A social-media platform recommends posts and a language model writes a summary of them.
sections: A phone suggests the next word while you type.
A language model learns statistical patterns of tokens; tokens may be words, parts of words or punctuation.
Given 'The weather is', a model may assign different scores to 'sunny', 'cold' and 'changing'.
A recommendation platform records which posts people click.
Large-scale data may contain preferences, biases, copyrighted materials and personal information. Having data does not always give permission to reuse it.
Two users who click on different posts can receive very different recommended content.
Someone watches three football videos, so the platform offers a fourth.
Recommenders may rank content based on observed behaviour; recommendation is not the same as knowing a person's intentions or values.
A click is a noisy signal: curiosity and disagreement can both cause clicks.
print('Clicks ≠ complete understanding of a person')
A generated answer invents a source it cannot actually provide.
Language-model output must be checked against evidence. Discuss hallucination, privacy, misinformation, environmental costs, labour and social impacts.
A confident-sounding claim without a verifiable source is still uncertain.
